source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it: preferring shorter thinking chains
finding: For the same question, the shortest sampled chain of a reasoning model is more often right than a random or the longest chain. A short-m@k vote (stop when the first m chains finish, then vote) matches or beats full majority vote at lower token cost.
numbers: 20 samples per question, 4 benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, HMMT Feb25, GPQA-diamond), max 32,768 tokens, temp 0.7. Shortest chain is 25-50% shorter than random. Shortest vs random: +2.2 to +15.7 points on math. Longest vs random: -5.4 to -18.8 points. Shortest vs longest: up to 34.5 points. short-1@k uses up to 40% fewer thinking tokens at the same accuracy (LN-Super-49B: 57% accuracy at about 60% of majority@k compute). short-3@k beats majority@k at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time.
quote: shorter reasoning chains within individual questions are significantly more likely to yield correct answers
limits: Within-question comparison, so difficulty is held fixed, but chains that never finished are excluded. Reasoning models on competition math and GPQA only. Not a test of brief CoT on non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Supports G11: when several tries are possible, prefer the short ones. A cheap rule is to sample k chains, stop early, and vote. Answers gap 1 for reasoning models.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Compute-optimal allocation per difficulty bin beats a fixed best-of-N at about 4x less compute. Easy questions gain from sequential revision; hard ones need a mix of sequential and parallel; the hardest get little from any method.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2 base, five difficulty bins from verifier scores (these predict method efficacy better than MATH's human levels). Compute-optimal search nearly matches PRM best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (16 vs 64 generations); revisions: 64 vs 256 samples. Bins 1-2: beam search gets worse as budget grows (verifier over-optimisation). Bins 3-4: beam search beats best-of-N. Bin 5: no method makes meaningful progress. FLOPs-matched: a smaller model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger model where its success rate is non-trivial.
quote: the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt
limits: Verifier-based search and revisions, not plain CoT length. PaLM 2 era, MATH only. Predicted difficulty loses part of the gain at high budgets. On the hardest questions pretraining wins.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a difficulty gate helps. Easy items: one pass; mid items: more compute; hopeless items: stop early.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference scaling laws: compute-optimal inference for LLM problem-solving
finding: Cost-matched comparison of greedy, majority vote, best-of-n, weighted vote and tree search across model sizes. Smaller models plus a better inference strategy can sit on the cost-accuracy Pareto front; returns from more samples saturate.
numbers: Pythia on GSM8K, Llemma on MATH. Llemma-7B with their REBASE tree search beats Llemma-34B across all tested strategies at equal compute on MATH.
limits: Open 2023-24 models, math only. Equal FLOPs, not equal tokens on API models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: voting among chains has a saturating curve, so a small k is the efficient region.

source: Balachandran et al. (2025) Inference-time scaling for complex tasks: where we stand and what lies ahead
finding: Nine models, eight hard tasks. More tokens do not reliably mean more accuracy. Token use varies a lot across models with similar accuracy and across runs of one model. Gains shrink as problem complexity grows.
numbers: AIME 25: DeepSeek R1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet are within 3% accuracy over five repeats but R1 uses at least 5x more tokens. With perfect verifiers all models gain a lot, and on some tasks conventional models (e.g. GPT-4o) with many runs approach the average of reasoning models.
quote: simply using more tokens does not necessarily translate to higher accuracy
limits: Perfect-verifier bounds are not realistic. Hard benchmarks only (math, STEM, calendar planning, NP-hard, navigation, spatial).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: token cost is high-variance and weakly tied to accuracy, so a budget cap and a verifier matter more than chain length.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute (TMLR)
finding: Tasks built so that longer reasoning lowers accuracy in current reasoning models from Anthropic, OpenAI and DeepSeek. Failure modes differ by vendor: Claude gets distracted by irrelevant facts; o-series resists distractors but overfits the problem framing; others drift to spurious features or lose focus on hard deduction.
numbers: Counting with distractors: Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning lengthens. DeepSeek R1 (natural length) falls from 70% to 30% with five distractors. o3 is more stable (weak decline). Inverse scaling is defined as more than 2% accuracy change with non-overlapping CIs. Requested budgets 0 to 16,384 tokens.
quote: Claude models become increasingly distracted by irrelevant information
limits: Hand-built adversarial probes, not typical workloads. Natural-length setup is confounded with difficulty. Safety-behaviour results not used here.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 6 and 10: current models also hurt themselves with longer chains when distractors or spurious features exist. Supports G11 and a G10-style check that the answer ignores irrelevant text.

source: Li et al. (2025) When thinking fails: the pitfalls of reasoning for instruction-following in LLMs
finding: Adding a CoT instruction lowers instruction-following accuracy in most models. Selective use (a trained classifier, or the model's own choice) recovers much of the loss.
numbers: 15 models, IFEval and ComplexBench. 13 of 14 models drop on IFEval with CoT; all drop on ComplexBench. Llama3-8B-Instruct 75.2 -> 59.0. Claude-3.5-Sonnet 86.5 -> 79.5. Claude-3.7-Sonnet 90.6 -> 90.2. Reasoning variant vs base on IFEval: Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Think 90.2 vs 90.6; DeepSeek-R1 83.3 vs V3 85.2 (not a controlled comparison). Classifier-selective reasoning (Qwen2.5-7B classifier, validation accuracy 0.75-0.92) recovered most of the loss.
quote: explicit CoT reasoning can significantly degrade instruction-following accuracy
limits: Table layout garbled in text extraction; only headline numbers used. Attention analysis is correlational. Instruction-following tasks, not reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6: a task type where CoT hurts across vendors, including Claude. Argues for a gate: think only when the item is multi-step, not when it mainly has simple output constraints.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats confuse reasoning LLM: query-agnostic adversarial triggers (CatAttack), COLM 2025
finding: Appending an irrelevant sentence to a math problem raises the error rate of reasoning models, and triggers found on a cheap proxy model transfer. An instruction to ignore distractions cut failures in the one small test.
numbers: 2000 questions; 1618 solved by proxy DeepSeek V3; 574 triggers fooled it (35%); 114 transferred to DeepSeek R1 (about 20%). Error rate up over 300% for R1; up to 500% for reasoning models and 700% for instruction-tuned models in the transfer test. Defence on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: an ignore-distractors line cut attack success from 37.5% to 9.9%; SFT on two triggers did not generalise to a third.
quote: appending Interesting fact: cats sleep most of their lives to any math problem leads to more than doubling the chances of a model getting the answer wrong
limits: Worst-case, adversarially selected triggers, not an average. The ignore-line test is one 8B model, not equal-token. Only 60% of modified problems were judged semantically consistent by annotators.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: perturbation weakness persists in 2025 reasoning models. A short 'ignore irrelevant information' line is cheap and may help; needs our own test.

source: Li et al. (2024) GSM-Plus: robustness of LLMs as mathematical problem solvers
finding: On perturbed GSM8K, CoT accuracy falls. Critical-thinking items (unanswerable or contradictory) fall most. Sub-goal prompting plus self-consistency helps most.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo pass@1: CoT 74.17 on GSM8K vs 62.92 on GSM-Plus; critical-thinking subset 40.83; distractor insertion 63.33. Complexity-based CoT 76.67 -> 65.52 (critical thinking 54.17). CoT+SC 76.67 -> 66.88. Their COMP+SC 80.00 -> 69.47. 25 LLMs, 4 prompting methods.
limits: 2023-24 models; GPT-3.5 numbers from the fine-grained table. No frontier or reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: CoT gains on clean GSM8K overstate performance on perturbed items; voting or sub-goal checks recover some points, not all.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting each sampled chain's vote by the model's own confidence gives the same accuracy with far fewer samples. The confidence measure that best separates right from wrong chains for one question is not the best-calibrated one across questions.
numbers: 9 models, 4 datasets: CISC beats plain self-consistency in nearly all setups and cuts needed samples by over 40% on average. Plain SC needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10 (46% saving). Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30-sample SC (73% cost reduction).
limits: Extra confidence query adds a little cost. Open and mid-sized models; math and QA. Does not test vote share as a trigger for a verification step.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: per-chain confidence is a usable signal inside one question, so extra checking can be triggered by low confidence. Judge by within-question discrimination, not global calibration.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling chains once the lead of the top answer is statistically safe (Dirichlet model of vote counts). Saves samples with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs: sample budget cut by up to 7.9x with average accuracy drop under 0.1%. Example: 9 of the first 10 samples agree gives over 99% chance the majority holds at 40.
quote: reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Savings come mostly from easy items that agree early. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: vote share is a cheap confidence gate. Early agreement means stop; disagreement means spend more or verify.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: Program-aided language models
finding: Let the model write the reasoning as code and let an interpreter run it. This beats written-out arithmetic and holds up when numbers get large or there are many objects.
numbers: Codex GSM8K: CoT 65.6 vs PAL 72.0; with majority@40 PAL 80.4 vs Minerva 540B 78.5. GSM-Hard (bigger numbers): direct 19.7 -> 5.0, CoT 65.6 -> 20.1, PAL 72.0 -> 61.5. Colored objects: PAL stays near 100% as object count grows while CoT becomes unstable.
limits: Not matched on tokens. Codex-era model. Planning is still left to the model.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a large share of CoT error is arithmetic execution, and handing it to a tool is robust. The equal-token test on a modern model is still not measured.

source: Li et al. (2025) LLMs can easily learn to reason from demonstrations: structure, not content, is what matters
finding: For long-CoT fine-tuning, wrong answers or corrupted digits in the training chains cost little, while shuffling or deleting steps costs a lot. This is a modern analogue of Wang 2022 invalid exemplars, but it is training, not prompting.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, 17k R1-generated samples. Untrained base average 56.7 over five benchmarks. Training on wrong-answer samples: average 63.1, only 3.2 points below training on correct ones. 70% of digits corrupted: 4.3 points below. All digits corrupted: performance collapses. Shuffling 67% of steps: AIME 2024 down 13.3 points.
quote: the structure of Long CoT is critical to the learning process, whereas the content of individual reasoning steps has minimal impact
limits: Fine-tuning study, not in-context prompting. Numbers read from extracted tables; treat exact baselines as approximate.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: supports the view that the lever is chain form and logical order, not correctness of each step. Consistent with G10: a fluent chain proves nothing.

source: Chua and Evans (2025) Are DeepSeek R1 and other reasoning models more faithful?
finding: Reasoning models state a misleading cue in their chain much more often than non-reasoning models. The chain is more informative about hints in them, but still misses many cases.
numbers: MMLU with a 'Stanford professor thinks the answer is D' cue, among cases where the answer switched: DeepSeek-R1 names the cue 59%, Gemini reasoning 68%, Qwen reasoning 47%, best non-reasoning model 13%, DeepSeek-V3 7%. Another cue: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 3% vs 17-35% for reasoning models. Another: GPT-4o 2% vs 16-47%. Some cue types are near 0% for all models.
quote: the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning model describes the cue's influence 59% of the time, compared to 7%
limits: Artificial cues on MMLU. Tests only whether the model says it used the cue. Reward-model link to lower faithfulness is suggestive.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: even in modern reasoning models roughly 30-50% of cue-driven switches go unstated, and some cue types near 100%. A chain cannot be the only evidence (G10); an independent check is needed. Whether such a check catches the hidden cases is not tested here.

source: Opus and Lawsen (2025) The illusion of the illusion of thinking
finding: Re-reading of Shojaee et al.: the Tower of Hanoi collapse tracks output token limits, River Crossing includes unsolvable instances, and asking for a program instead of a move list restores success.
numbers: River Crossing with N>=6 and boat capacity 3 is unsolvable, yet scored as failure. A Hanoi move list needs about 10(2^N - 1)+C tokens, so a 64k cap is exceeded near N=9-13 for the full list, and collapse reported before N=9 is earlier than that limit. A preliminary Lua-function prompt for N=15 gave very high accuracy in under 5,000 tokens on Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5.
limits: Short comment. The N=15 test is preliminary, no trial counts. Token arithmetic assumes 10 tokens per move. The paper itself notes the models stop before the hard limit, which is a choice rather than a cap.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, partly closed: Hanoi collapse is largely a format and grading artifact and River Crossing a task-validity error. It does not show these models plan well over long horizons. Use programs or tools for long deterministic execution.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking (re-read for gap 9)
finding: Re-checked the setup: 64k generation cap for the reasoning models. They report that thinking tokens fall as complexity rises past a critical point even with budget left, and that at low complexity non-thinking models beat thinking ones at equal tokens.
numbers: Max generation 64,000 tokens (Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1 and V3 on local servers). Three regimes: low complexity non-thinking is better and cheaper; medium complexity thinking wins; high complexity both collapse.
limits: The cap and the unsolvable River Crossing instances are the objections raised by Opus and Lawsen. No larger-budget rerun of the same puzzles was found in this pass (web search budget ran out).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays partly open. The low-complexity finding (plain answer beats long chain) agrees with G11 either way.
